families.name: Artifacts-based Detection
families.definition: Methods that identify tampering by analyzing low-level statistical inconsistencies or sensor-specific noise patterns left behind by image processing operations.

properties.text: These methods rely on the assumption that digital manipulation disrupts the natural statistical correlations present in authentic images.
They often utilize Error Level Analysis (ELA) or noise residual analysis to detect regions with inconsistent compression histories.
The approach is model-agnostic and does not require prior knowledge of the specific editing tool used.
They are particularly effective for detecting copy-move forgery and splicing in JPEG-compressed images.
The detection signal is derived from the physical or algorithmic footprint of the manipulation process itself.

limitations.text: Performance degrades significantly when the manipulated image undergoes additional compression or resizing after the initial tampering.
These methods struggle to distinguish between benign post-processing (like cropping or rotation) and malicious editing.
They are generally ineffective against deepfake generation models that synthesize pixels from scratch rather than manipulating existing ones.
The method is sensitive to the specific parameters of the compression algorithm, requiring careful calibration.
It cannot provide semantic context for the detected anomaly, only indicating where an inconsistency exists.

families.name: Metadata-based Detection
families.definition: Techniques that examine the header information and embedded data of media files to identify inconsistencies or signs of manipulation.

properties.text: This approach analyzes EXIF data, file headers, and embedded watermarks to verify the provenance and history of the media.
It is computationally efficient and can provide immediate results without processing the pixel data.
The method is deterministic, relying on the presence or absence of specific metadata fields.
It is highly effective for detecting simple edits where metadata is not properly stripped or updated.
It serves as a quick pre-filter for more complex pixel-based analysis.

limitations.text: Metadata can be easily stripped or forged by standard image editing software and online tools.
Many social media platforms automatically remove or alter metadata upon upload, rendering this method useless for shared content.
It provides no insight into the visual content of the image, only its file structure.
The method is binary in nature, offering no confidence score for the degree of tampering.
It is completely ineffective against deepfakes generated by neural networks that create new files without inheriting original metadata.

families.name: Frequency-domain Analysis
families.definition: Methods that transform image data into the frequency domain to detect spectral anomalies introduced by manipulation or synthesis.

properties.text: These techniques use transforms like the Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) or Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) to analyze the distribution of frequencies.
They are effective at detecting blurring, sharpening, and interpolation artifacts that are invisible in the spatial domain.
The method can identify the specific type of interpolation used during resizing, which is a common step in forgery.
It is robust to minor spatial domain noise that might obscure spatial-based artifacts.
The analysis focuses on the global or local spectral characteristics of the image.

limitations.text: The method is sensitive to the specific parameters of the frequency transform used, requiring consistent preprocessing.
It can be confused by natural textures that have similar spectral properties to manipulated regions.
It does not provide semantic understanding of the image content, only statistical spectral deviations.
Performance is affected by the quality of the original image, as low-quality sources have less distinct spectral signatures.
It is less effective against high-quality deepfakes that are designed to mimic natural frequency distributions.

families.name: Deep Learning-based Detection
families.definition: Neural network models trained to learn the high-level features and patterns that distinguish authentic media from manipulated or synthesized media.

properties.text: These methods use Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) or Vision Transformers to learn complex, non-linear representations of image data.
They can detect subtle, high-level inconsistencies that are imperceptible to human eyes and traditional statistical methods.
The approach is data-driven, requiring large datasets of labeled authentic and tampered images for training.
It is highly effective for detecting deepfakes, as it can learn the specific artifacts introduced by generative models like GANs.
The model can be fine-tuned for specific types of manipulation or specific generative models.

limitations.text: The method requires significant computational resources for both training and inference.
It is prone to overfitting if the training data is not diverse enough, leading to poor generalization to unseen manipulations.
The model is a black box, making it difficult to interpret why a specific image was classified as fake.
It is vulnerable to adversarial attacks where small, imperceptible perturbations are added to fool the detector.
The performance degrades when the test data distribution differs significantly from the training data distribution.

families.name: Biometric-based Detection
families.definition: Techniques that verify the authenticity of media by analyzing biometric features such as facial landmarks, eye blinks, and physiological signals.

properties.text: This approach focuses on the consistency of biometric features across frames in video or within a single image.
It is particularly effective for detecting face swaps and deepfakes by analyzing the geometry and texture of facial features.
The method can detect unnatural movements, such as lack of eye blinking or inconsistent lip synchronization.
It relies on the assumption that human biometric features follow specific physiological and anatomical constraints.
It is often used in conjunction with other methods to provide a higher level of confidence.

limitations.text: The method is limited to media containing recognizable biometric features, such as faces or hands.
It is less effective for detecting non-biometric tampering, such as object insertion or background modification.
High-quality deepfakes can mimic natural biometric movements, making them difficult to detect using this method alone.
The method is sensitive to lighting, pose, and occlusion, which can affect the accuracy of biometric feature extraction.
It does not provide information about the specific tool or technique used to create the forgery.

Designing detection techniques that are resilient to adversarial attacks and data poisoning.
